### [101] [RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19705)
*Xiaohan Wang,Haozhen Zhang,Qingyuan Liu,Tao Feng,Wenya Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

### [102] [BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19704)
*Md Rayhanul Masud,S M Maksudul Alam,Mohammad Jaminur Islam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: this https URL .

### [103] [Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19696)
*Xin Li,Mengbing Liu,Hao Jiang,Xin Gao,Annan Wang,Xingwei Qu,Yichi Zhang,Chau Yuen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

### [104] [Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19644)
*Bin Zheng,Zheng Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

### [105] [J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19638)
*Chihiro Yano,Jun Hirako,Hiroaki Yamagiwa,Ryota Hirobuchi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

### [106] [Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19613)
*Oscar Chew,Po-Yi Lu,Yi-Jie Cheng,Kunal Jain,Hsuan-Tien Lin,Zhengzhong Tu,Kuan-Hao Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

### [107] [PA1-OPD: One-Step Prefix-Augmented On-Policy Distillation for Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19601)
*Zhenhe Wu,Jian Yang,Yaping Jin,Xinlai Kang,Jie Hu,Hanting Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.

### [108] [Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19587)
*Adel Khorramrouz,Yi-Chia Wang,Sharon Levy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.

</details>


### [109] [GraphRAG-LTM: A Layered Threat Modeling Framework for Attacks on Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19549)
*Yining Tang,Junyu Zhang,Haomiao Qiu,Yongchao Liu,Jiajun Zheng,Zhao Wang,Ziyue Qiao,Chao Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) uses document-derived knowledge graphs to assemble evidence for large language model (LLM) answers. Its security depends on both the seed chunks retrieved for a query and the graph evidence assembled from them, yet attacks on this evidence path remain underexplored. We introduce GraphRAG-LTM, a Layered Threat Modeling framework that tests three nested levels of attacker access. BB Query uses ranking feedback to make query edits under a semantic-similarity constraint and demote relevant seed chunks. WB Query uses retriever gradients for the same objective. Graph-aware WB keeps the white-box adversarial query and deletes bridge triplets from the query-specific evidence graph, disrupting multi-hop evidence propagation through localized graph edits. Across datasets, retrievers, and LLM backbones, rank feedback alone reduces answer quality, gradient access strengthens query attacks, and bridge-triplet deletion further impairs supporting-fact retrieval. Further analyses show how seed retrieval and graph evidence jointly contribute to these failures.

### [110] [One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19510)
*Yangyi Shen,Pin-Jui Ku,Nicolai Oswald,Jean-Marie Lemercier,Yonggan Fu,Stefano Ermon,Jure Leskovec,Boris Ginsburg,Ante Jukić*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

### [111] [Towards Efficient Simultaneous Inverse Text Normalization with Pretrained Text-to-Text Language Model and Read-Tag-Write Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19492)
*Kiet Anh Hoang,Khanh Le,Bao Nguyen,Linh Pham,Dung Vo,Thai Tran,Mai Nguyen,Tri Nguyen,Vu Le*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Streaming Inverse Text Normalization (ITN) is vital for converting spoken-form outputs from streaming Automatic Speech Recognition into formatted written text. Existing streaming ITN methods rely on hybrid systems combining neural tagging with expert-crafted finite-state transducer rules, limiting scalability across domains and languages. While end-to-end models offer superior scalability by learning directly from data, standard encoder-decoder architectures are inherently non-streaming due to global attention. In this paper, we propose an efficient streaming end-to-end ITN system, adapting a pretrained text-to-text model to leverage its robust linguistic knowledge. To enable streaming, we introduce architectural adaptations, a specialized training strategy, a Read-Tag-Write decoding policy, and inference optimizations. Experiments on Vietnamese datasets show accuracy comparable to non-streaming baselines, outperforming hybrid methods while satisfying real-time latency requirements.

### [112] [AgriJev: Efficient Agricultural Candidate Scoring with Multi-Scale Adapted Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19478)
*Xuechen Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Agricultural systems make decisions over heterogeneous entity types, textual judgments, and knowledge-question options. Generating a textual answer adds decoding and extraction steps to decisions that ultimately require a candidate choice. We introduce AgriJev, a family of adapted Qwen3.5 models at 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B. A shared interface conditions on agricultural text, a judgment question, and candidate definitions, returning scores and relative probabilities in one forward call. We prepare source-aware training records and frozen evaluations from existing agricultural resources, retaining original groups and annotation provenance. Comparisons include original Qwen3.5 models and matched agricultural SFT models, both evaluated through native answer generation. Across 17 external test views, AgriJev-9B reaches 75.44% mean accuracy, exceeding the original and SFT generators by 5.89 and 3.79 percentage points. It outperforms the original generator on 13 views and narrows the mean gap to hosted Jev 1.13.0. On a fixed A100 workload, its median scoring latency is approximately half that of same-scale answer generation. Task-dependent gains and failures characterize a practical choice among agricultural model weights and inference contracts.

### [113] [More Than Seeing: Vision as Scalable Anchors in Native Multimodal Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19443)
*Haoyuan Wu,Aoqi Wu,Jiani Hu,Bei Yu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

### [114] [ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19408)
*Zhaoyan Jia,Chengwei Zhou,Gourav Datta,Massoud Pedram*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

### [115] [The Sum of All Summaries: PROPALIGN for Graded Proposition Salience Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19387)
*Lin Ai,Emma Thronson,Katherine Conhaim,Amir Zeldes*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Identification and ranking of salient propositions in documents is indirectly involved in many AI tasks, but few papers define proposition salience scores clearly, make diverse data available, or evaluate models directly on the task. This paper proposes PROPALIGN, a multiple-summary-based approach for propositional salience score estimation, and releases PROPALIGNBANK, an accompanying dataset for the method with 138K alignments of over 35K propositions. We compare several approaches to salient proposition extraction in English across a broad range of spoken and written genres, and demonstrate that naively asking models for judgments leads to inconsistencies. By contrast, graded, summary-based metrics are more stable. We further observe that while single models perform worse than humans, an ensemble of models incorporating linguistic features approaches manual annotation quality ceilings. In addition, analyses of the model outputs suggest insights into how models can extract salient information with and without the use of summaries.

### [116] [Learning What to Keep: Transfer-Aware Personal Skill Learning from User Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19380)
*Li Wang,Chen Zhang,Yirong Yang,Xingyu Chen,Jinkun Zhao,Tianhao Peng,Wenjun Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

### [117] [PersEvalBench: Can LLM Evaluators Judge Contextually Appropriate Use of Persona Information?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19314)
*Xinyi Liu,Hooshang Nayyeri,Emine Yilmaz,Dilek Hakkani-Tur,Charith Peris,Hari Thadakamalla*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable. Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

### [118] [Qwenfant: Train Big Character-level BabyLMs on Concise Parallel Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19294)
*Lukas Edman,Alexander Fraser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

### [119] [Can LLM Agents Efficiently Identify Appliance Faults? Insights From Diagnosing a Simulated Appliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19291)
*Lucas H. McCabe,Sarah Lukens,H. Howie Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).

### [120] [DUALVIEW: Leveraging Broad and Output-Specific Evidence for LLM-based Multi-Output Text Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19206)
*Yiheng Su,Junyi Jessy Li,Matthew Lease*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.

### [121] [Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19202)
*Zixuan Liu,Gustavo Didier,Fangzheng Wu,Brian Summa,Zizhan Zheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

Abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

</details>


### [122] [NEPSEE: A Double-Annotated Benchmark for Nepali Sentiment Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19190)
*Gaurab Baral,Mimansak Nepal,Grishma Basnet*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Many sentiment datasets use one annotator for each item, so the test labels show the conventions of that person. We build a Nepali benchmark from two annotators who labelled the same sentences blind. They labelled 5,614 sentences from tweets of Nepali public figures on a five-point scale. We keep only the 3,189 sentences where both give the same polarity. On the three-class benchmark, NepBERTa with a fixed tokenizer gets a macro-F1 of 0.877 and IndicBERTv2 0.867. Three commercial large language models (LLMs) get 0.882 to 0.896 zero-shot, and these differences are not significant. On the five-point scale, 766 sentences have two adjacent labels, for example Pos and SPos. We accept both labels and train on both. On this task, Claude Opus 5.5 beats the best encoders by 0.10 to 0.12 macro-F1. A tokenizer audit adds a second result. The default tokenizers of three Nepali BERT models delete the non-spacing Devanagari vowel signs and the virama. When we restore the marks, macro-F1 increases by 0.084 for NepBERTa but decreases by 0.095 for a model pretrained on stripped text.

### [123] [How to Evaluate When You Don't Know How to Evaluate? Choosing Reliable Setups for Base Language Model Benchmarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19185)
*Shenbin Qian,David Samuel,Jindřich Helcl,Andrey Kutuzov,Stephan Oepen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.

### [124] [HERO: Harnessing Evidence for Test-time Refinement and Prompt Optimization in Program Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19184)
*Mingyu Lu,Timothy Ossowski,Tristan Naumann,Hoifung Poon,Peniel Argaw*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Harness optimization improves LLMs by refining reusable prompts and scaffolding, yet requires further adaptation for program generation tasks such as text-to-SQL and text-to-Python. Existing methods often rely on LLM reflectors to propose harness updates, which can fix observed failures but also disrupt previously correct behavior. Text-to-code tasks offer a natural way to mitigate this issue: we can execute generated outputs, allowing us to evaluate and verify the effects of proposed updates directly. Building on this signal, we introduce \textsc{HERO} (\textbf{H}arnessing \textbf{E}vidence for \textbf{R}efinement and \textbf{O}ptimization), which combines offline and test-time harness optimization. At the first stage, \method{} learns reusable prompt updates from execution-verified successes and failures and validates candidate revisions before adoption. At test time, we treat the generated code as an instance-specific harness and refine it using execution feedback. Across four SQL, Cypher, and Python benchmarks, \method{} achieves the best offline performance, improving pass@1 by \(7.6\) points over the initial prompt, while test-time refinement adds another \(2.0\) points and improves execution efficiency.

### [125] [Fantastic Metrics and How to Find Them: Meta-Evaluating Metrics for Multi-lingual Style-Personalized Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19166)
*Anubhav Jangra,Adrian de Wynter*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Meta-evaluation of text generation metrics and LLM-judges is primarily conducted using metric-human correlations. However, prior work has shown that correlation is not an appropriate estimate of a metric's evaluation capability and can be unstable across evaluation settings, such as different datasets or languages. Therefore, we propose a regression-based meta-evaluation of metrics that learns on calibrated metric outputs to predict human ratings. We ground this measurement relative to a trivial constant-mean baseline and human agreements to provide a comparable measure of metric capability across evaluation settings. To test our meta-evaluation framework, we developed a large-scale multi-lingual style-personalized text generation (SPTG) benchmark, collecting multiple annotations across 10 topologically diverse languages and four evaluation dimensions, each with varying degrees of subjectivity. We meta-evaluated 32 metrics from three style evaluation paradigms (string-based, embedding-based, and LLM-judges) and their ensembles over these 40 evaluation settings. Our analysis revealed that even simple string- and embedding-based measurements can match strong LLM-judges when calibrated to human ratings. We also identified characteristics of human annotations that determine metric performance, as well as conditions under which a metric ensemble outperforms its individual constituents.

### [126] [From Qualitative Text to Integrated Evidence: The Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI) Procedure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19164)
*Elyas Irankhah,Ashley Hagaman,Samah Fodeh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Mixed methods research offers established strategies for integrating qualitative and quantitative evidence, but less guidance for integrating two computational representations of the same qualitative corpus. This methodological study introduces Parallel-Then-Integrated (PTI), a four-step procedure for explicit and traceable integration. We present PTI using 1,203 interview paragraphs from 29 mothers in Nepal. The two representations were ontology-guided Patient Voice (PV) coding with PVminer and data-driven themes generated through non-negative matrix factorization (NMF). A theme-complete crosswalk documented convergence, divergence, and preprocessing-sensitive differences. Depression status, based on Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scores, served as a secondary external anchor for exploratory association checks. PTI provides a structured approach for integrating computational representations of qualitative text within mixed methods research.

### [127] [DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19118)
*Yifan Lan,Zhongye Liu,Yurui Chang,Hanyu Wang,Yongkang Du,Lu Lin,Jinghui Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at this https URL .

### [128] [Pre-Trained Language Models as Zero-Shot Tools for Social Science Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19048)
*Noah Dasanaike*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Record linkage and demographic inference from names are routine demands in social science. Most approaches to these problems require labeled training data that are difficult or costly to acquire. I show that pre-trained language models perform both tasks accurately without requiring task-specific training. For record linkage, I introduce EnsembleLink, an algorithm that uses pre-trained embeddings alongside string-based scorers to retrieve a short list of candidates and then identify the likeliest matches. EnsembleLink matches or exceeds the performance of most prior approaches while generalizing across scripts and formats that those methods are unable to handle. For ethnicity inference from names, I show that large language models (LLMs) achieve up to 83.8% accuracy on U.S. voter files, compared to 78.0% for name-supplemented BISG. Open-weight models offer reproducible implementations that approach these models in accuracy. Moreover, LLMs are able to infer group membership for religious, caste-based, and other ethnic group categories outside of the United States, and reduce bias in downstream estimates of geographic racial gaps. Where pre-training encodes the world knowledge required by each task, task-specific labels add less information.

### [129] [Crossing the Gender Binary: Modelling Gendered Reference in Science Fiction and General Fiction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19028)
*Yuxuan Liu,Haim Dubossarsky,Ruth Ahnert*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Science fiction is widely credited with unsettling gender. This article asks whether that holds at the linguistic level, in how readily gendered reference gives way to its counterpart, a neutral term, or other social category, and whether it separates the genre from general fiction. It does so by masking man/men, woman/women, and person/people across same-period science fiction and general fiction corpora and classifying RoBERTa's five likeliest substitutes by gender. Retention and displacement are permutation-tested over five resampling rounds, and the underlying sentences are read closely. Both corpora cross the gender binary in both directions, but unequally: where woman is masked, the model predicts a masculine term about twice as often as it predicts a feminine term where man is masked. Each mismatch marks a statistical surprise, a word the corpus did not expect there. Against this shared pattern, science fiction shows greater gender permeability than the general fiction corpus, placing man in feminine contexts more often than general fiction while the reverse rate holds steady. Its degendering tendency is stronger too, drawing both gendered terms toward the neutral. Beyond the binary, a masked woman also draws substitutes naming a social category and no gender far more often than a masked man does. In measuring the gender permeability of man, woman, and person in linguistic distribution and testing whether genre changes it, the study gives science fiction studies linguistic evidence for thematic claims and computational literary studies a pipeline applicable to other category vocabularies, such as race and class.

### [130] [Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19026)
*Jiwon Song,Yoongon Kim,Jae-Joon Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.

### [131] [Can LLMs Access their World Knowledge for Event Prediction?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19021)
*Zijun Wu,Zhitian Zhang,Hossein Hajimirsadeghi,Nikita Dvornik,Alexander Pashevich*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Recent work has questioned whether large language models (LLMs) can be useful for temporal event prediction. Despite vast pretrained world knowledge, LLMs often underperform simpler specialized models. We ask whether this knowledge is truly inaccessible, or whether current methods fail to present event prediction in a form LLMs can use. We argue for the latter and show that LLMs become effective event forecasters when the interface is designed around two choices. The first grounds each event in a natural-language description, and the second separates event semantics from the prediction space to prevent semantic bias from label associations. To test this, we introduce DescribeEvent, a benchmark of ~150K events across seven datasets and six domains with event-level descriptions. We find that capable LLMs substantially benefit from descriptions and symbolic labels, outperforming description-free variants and non-LLM baselines, while weaker models gain little. These results suggest that accessing LLM world knowledge for event prediction is an interface problem, and that event descriptions offer a practical way to elicit the knowledge LLMs already encode.

### [132] [Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20344)
*Yuyao Ge,Shenghua Liu,Peizhong Gao,Chendi Ge,Chenxu Liu,Yiwei Wang,Lingrui Mei,Baolong Bi,Jiayu Yao,Jiafeng Guo,Xueqi Cheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Doc2Harness 是首个针对 LLM 长周期 harness 工程能力的确定性基准。它采用两阶段设计：第一阶段让被评估的构建模型基于开发文档和仅声明接口的合约骨架，在隔离容器中构建完整的候选 harness；第二阶段在独立容器中用脚本化的 mock 模型驱动冻结的候选 harness,通过四个可观察通道(模型请求、磁盘文件、进程退出码、命令输出)对 328 个测试用例进行评分,并用正向控制排除空通过。评测覆盖 19 个前沿模型各 3 次构建,GPT-6 Astra 最高通过率 53.05%,最弱模型仅 27.44%;分析表明高通过率的候选 harness 倾向于将横切关注点集中在更少的模块中。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 现有基准多在固定 harness 下衡量下游任务成功率,而 harness 本身的工程能力(决定模型能力有多少能传递到环境)未被直接评测。Harness 是近年才出现且更新频繁的代码对象,基于成熟仓库的 SWE 基准存在数据污染风险,且单元测试式评判标准不适用于 harness 这类同一特征可有多样内部实现、且需由模型驱动才能评估正确性的对象。

Method: 两阶段协议:Stage 1 在固定 builder harness(OpenCode 1.17.0)内,模型根据从 12 个前沿 harness 用户文档归并去歧得到的开发文档,以及从 mini-swe-agent 蒸馏的仅含三个外部接口(CLI、headless 入口、驱动评测 API)的合约骨架,在 2 小时/3 次提交配额内构建候选 harness;合同检查仅验证形式(可编译安装、命令齐备、无占位桩)。Stage 2 将候选 harness 冻结,在独立容器中由脚本化 mock 模型逐用例驱动,通过四个观测通道评分;针对每个共享观测前置条件的用例组设置正向控制(channel/same form/reverse 三类),以排除"特性未运行"导致的空通过。测试用例合成采用三方法循环:公开 issue 挖掘(从 4 个前沿 harness 共 21,083 条 issue 聚类筛选)、跨 harness 对比(将候选 harness 按开发文档章节切分后与成熟实现逐模块比对)、单变量扩展(围绕已通过/失败的种子用例一次只改一个变量:工具/输入形式/错误参数/返回位点)。统计上报告 328 个用例在 9 个互斥类别上的通过率、强弱差、判别用例数,以及 KR-20 内部一致性(0.913)。

Result: 主要结果:GPT-6 Astra 53.05%±0.25、Opus 5 46.65%±1.80、Qwen3.8 Max 45.83%±0.14、GPT-5.6-sol 43.80%±2.43、Grok 4.7 43.50%±2.49;最弱 Hy3 27.44%±0.43,跨度约 26 个百分点;强模型仍近半数用例失败,基准未饱和且具区分力。分维度:交互式终端近乎饱和(均 79.9%);权限最强区分度(强弱差 50.8,51/61 判别用例);GPT-6 Astra 与 Opus 5 在常规场景(72.46% vs 80.68%)与边界场景(48.97% vs 37.02%)互有领先。架构分析:代码行数与通过率相关 0.614(模型均值 0.629),代码行数方差 95.9% 来自模型间;控制代码行数后,模块数与通过率偏相关 −0.423,行/模块偏相关 +0.504,验证过瘦的文件继续分裂得越分散、通过率越低。六主类别间两两相关均为正(均值 +0.521),与总分相关 0.69–0.94,表明能力近似一维,但同一模型在六类间排名最大波动达 16 位。56 个用例被所有候选 harness 失败(地板用例),16 个被全部通过(天花板用例)。

Conclusion: Doc2Harness 是首个可确定性评估"模型开发 harness 能力"的基准,通过 mock 模型脚本化驱动 + 多通道观测 + 正向控制,实现了对 harness 自身行为逐条合规的判定。实验揭示两类信号:(1) 强模型仍失败近半,长周期 harness 工程远未被解决;(2) 失败并非随机,而集中于"横切功能如何在模块间划分"这一架构选择——更少、更大的模块与更高通过率显著相关。该基准为衡量此类构建能力提供了可靠工具。

Abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.

</details>


### [133] [SWE-Stream: Scaling Executable Training Data for SWE Agents via Progressive Construction and Elastic Streaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20193)
*Chengyang Liu,Wen Yang,Shifeng Chen,Delai Qiu,Ji Yang,Junnan Zhu,Yining Wang,Shengping Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: 本文提出SWE-Stream系统，通过渐进式构建和弹性流式执行来扩展可执行的软件工程训练数据。从10,728个仓库的203,905个PR候选中构建了80,874个验证任务，并在六种编程语言上收集了118,688条成功轨迹。微调Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507后在SWE-bench Verified、Multilingual和Pro上分别达到69.0%、49.3%和45.42%的解决率。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 软件工程代理训练受限于高质量可执行任务的稀缺。开发历史虽然包含丰富信号，但常因环境不完整、测试缺失和工件不一致而需要大量重建。现有方法存在候选重建异构、阶段同步屏障造成延迟、统一资源限制难以适配不同工作负载等问题。

Method: SWE-Stream采用两大核心设计：(1)渐进式任务构建——从仓库和PR筛选到构建完成，根据阶段结果决定候选是推进、针对性补全还是拒绝，优先复用已有工件；(2)弹性流式执行——调度器在共享资源预算下异步分发就绪阶段，结合压力准入控制、自适应资源限制和OOM恢复机制。系统基于mini-swe-agent 2.2.7和DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731构建。

Result: 从203,905个初始PR中筛选出117,663个候选，最终接受80,874个任务。环境重建成功率92.89%，测试准备85.99%，独立执行验证89.67%。微调后SWE-bench Verified解决率69.0%，Multilingual 49.3%，Pro 45.42%。在预算匹配对比中以45.6%优于三个现有数据源。流式构建吞吐量是批式构建的1.45倍，接受任务数比固定限制流式多13.2%。

Conclusion: SWE-Stream通过渐进式构建和弹性流式执行的组合，能够高效大规模地生成可执行的SWE训练数据，在六种编程语言上均有效。实验证明该数据在提升SWE代理性能和构建效率两方面均优于现有数据源和批式构建方法。

Abstract: Software engineering agents have advanced rapidly, but scaling their training remains constrained by the limited availability of high-quality executable tasks. Development histories contain valuable signals for constructing such tasks, yet they often require substantial reconstruction due to incomplete environments, missing tests, and inconsistent artifacts. We present SWE-Stream, a system for scaling executable SWE training data through progressive construction and elastic streaming execution. SWE-Stream progressively validates and refines task candidates, reusing existing artifacts when possible and applying targeted completion only when necessary. An elastic scheduler asynchronously coordinates construction stages under shared resource constraints, adapting execution budgets based on observed workload demands. Using development histories from 10,728 repositories across six programming languages, SWE-Stream constructs 80,874 validated tasks and collects 118,688 successful trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 on these trajectories achieves resolve rates of 69.0%, 49.3%, and 45.42% on SWE-bench Verified, Multilingual, and Pro, respectively. In a controlled comparison with approximately matched training budgets, SWE-Stream achieves a 45.6% resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming three existing data sources. Moreover, its streaming construction strategy improves efficiency, delivering $1.45\times$ the accepted-task throughput of batch construction and accepting 13.2% more tasks than fixed-limit streaming.

</details>


### [134] [SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20038)
*Songwei Yu,Ziqi Miao,Jingxuan Xu,Junhao Fan,Haoyang Huang,Yuan Xiong,Zihang Xu,Weihao Li,Wenqiang Zhu,Yuechen Luo,Xinshun Feng,Yanan Wu,Ken Deng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SWE-Nexus是一个全自动化的四智能体流水线，通过测试执行构建仓库级软件工程任务（原子任务与组合任务），构建了包含600个跨六种语言任务的基准，并评估了12个模型在三种智能体框架下的表现，最佳配置单次尝试解决率为37.8%。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 传统的基于历史PR的仓库级基准（如SWE-bench）存在三个核心问题：(1) 同一PR中的代码和测试不能揭示每个测试实际执行了哪些实现函数；(2) 历史补丁提取可能包含不相关的测试；(3) 固定的任务集合会因训练数据污染而失去评估价值，且无法覆盖跨文件/跨模块的组合行为需求。这些问题促使作者探索能否通过测试执行来自动构建超越单个PR边界的、具有多样化挑战性的仓库级任务。

Method: 方法采用四智能体全自动流水线：(1) Selector Agent从预筛选池中选择测试文件；(2) Trace Agent执行测试，通过运行时跟踪（Python用pytest回调、Go用函数入口插桩、JS/TS用源码插桩、Kotlin/Java用探针或字节码插桩）将测试映射到生产函数体，形成"观察执行足迹"(S_t)；(3) Validation Agent适配执行协议和结果解析器，独立验证程序仅保留满足"原始仓库所有评分点通过"且"遮蔽后至少一个失败/错误"的作用域；(4) Query Agent从原始实现和测试生成行为规范。组合阶段对来自同一仓库版本和环境的兼容作用域取并集（共享函数去重），并重新验证每个组成测试文件。最终形成原子任务（单测试文件）和组合任务（2-9个测试文件）。评估指标包括解决率（严格通过所有评分点）和作用域加权分数（按函数体源行数对评分点加权）。

Result: 构建了600个任务（105个仓库，六种语言各100个），包含116个原子任务和484个组合任务。每个任务平均35个遮蔽函数体，参考恢复补丁中位数433行变更。评估12个模型（Claude Opus 4.8、Gemini 3.1 Pro、GPT-5.3/5.4/5.5、Qwen3.5-Plus、DeepSeek-V3.2/V4-Flash、GLM-5/5.2、Kimi K2.6、MiniMax-M2.7）在三种框架（Claude Code、Cline、OpenCode）下：Claude Opus 4.8在Claude Code下P@1解决率最高（37.8%），GPT-5.5在作用域加权分数上领先（59.7%）。难度梯度明显：Easy→Medium→Hard，平均解决率从55.2%降至7.4%。Java平均表现最好（37.1%），JavaScript最差（12.7%）。轨迹分析显示成功尝试的工具调用次数和修改文件数中位数更低。

Conclusion: SWE-Nexus通过测试执行验证而非历史PR边界来自动构建仓库级实现任务，实现了从原子到组合的多层次任务构建。作用域加权评分为部分恢复提供了细粒度度量，可作为强化学习的分级奖励。组合经过验证的执行足迹使任务能够跨越单个历史变更、覆盖多个函数和模块，为软件工程智能体的评估和训练提供了可扩展、污染抗性更强的基准。

Abstract: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.

</details>


### [135] [JevCoder: When Does Decision Delegation Pay Off in Code Repair?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19596)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yifan Zhang,Yu Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: JevCoder提出一个基于低成本概率判官Jev的代码修复工作流，通过在修复前进行代码片段推荐、修复中进行动作类型引导、以及根据模型规模采用不同的停止策略，使三种修复模型的token使用量减少21.6%-50.6%，同时修复率均有所提升。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 代码修复代理的多次决策影响修复轨迹和后续请求的token成本。论文探究哪些修复决策可以委托给低成本的概率判官，以减少token使用同时保持修复质量。动机源于工作流设计对推理成本的重大影响，以及同模型监督成本高但收益有限（SWE-PRM研究发现监督调用成本是修复调用的六倍多）。

Method: JevCoder结合三个组件：(1)代码片段推荐——修复前用Jev的相关性概率对候选片段排序，选择的片段保留在交互历史中；(2)动作类型引导——每次命令后用Jev判断修复状态（代码已定位/问题已复现/修复停滞/编辑后检查），程序规则将答案映射为动作建议（编辑/探测/测试/搜索）；(3)停止策略——大型API模型（DeepSeek/Gemini）观察到成功检查后自动提交，小型模型（Qwen）基于连续无进展判断提交。评估三个修复模型（DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash、Qwen3.8-27B-FP8、Gemini 3.8 Flash）在SWE-bench Verified和SWE-Bench Pro Verified各200个任务上的表现，并与无引导修复和同模型判官进行比较。

Result: JevCoder在400个任务上：DeepSeek修复率77.25%（基线76.25%），token减少21.6%，运行时减少10.5%；Qwen修复率46.75%（基线45.00%），token减少50.6%，运行时减少33.6%。所有修复率比较均满足预设的修复损失标准（95%区间下界≥-10pp）。Jev在判断质量上优于同模型判官：停滞修复AUROC 0.968 vs 0.931，成功检查信号AUROC 0.990 vs 0.974。片段推荐可减少5次修复前命令，保留片段比撤回可减少0.538M token。命令阻止组件未达修复损失标准，未被采纳。

Conclusion: 决策委托的有效性取决于干预改变了多少后续修复工作，而非单次判断的成本。Jev判官在修复状态判断上强于补丁结果预测。JevCoder通过组合片段推荐、动作类型引导和模型特定的停止策略，在三个不同规模的修复模型上一致地减少token使用并提高修复率，验证了低成本概率判官在代码修复代理中的实用价值。

Abstract: A coding agent repeatedly makes decisions as it repairs code. These decisions shape repair trajectories and affect the token cost of successive model requests. We ask which repair decisions can be delegated to a low-cost probabilistic judge to reduce token use while maintaining repair quality. The judges answer questions with probabilities over predefined answers, without generating explanations. We evaluate judgment quality across repair stages and test how individual interventions change subsequent repair work. We compare these interventions with unguided repair, which uses no judge, and with the same workflow using the repair model itself as the judge. The benefit depends on the work an intervention changes, rather than the cost of the judgment alone. Based on these studies, we propose JevCoder, a workflow built around Jev, a low-cost probabilistic judge. It combines code-snippet recommendations with action-type guidance and uses judgments to determine when to submit. We evaluate three repair models, each on the same 400 tasks: 200 from SWE-bench Verified and 200 from SWE-Bench Pro Verified. Compared to unguided repair, JevCoder reduces mean repair-model token use by 21.6%-50.6%, with higher observed repair rates across all three models.

</details>


### [136] [What Should a Software Team Spend on Agents? Simulation-Based Cost Optimization of Mixed AI-Human Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20394)
*Steffen Herbold*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Context: AI agents are rapidly adopted in software development, but their token costs are rising and it is unclear how much a team should spend on agents, and on which tasks. Objective: We determine how teams should divide spending between human developers and AI agents to deliver the features a project demands at the lowest total cost. Method: We model mixed teams of human developers and AI agents with eight specialized roles as a discrete-time stochastic process covering bug injection and detection, technical debt, human supervision of agents, and release cycles with feature freezes. Using Monte Carlo simulation and evolutionary search, we determine cost-optimal teams for 432 scenarios varying developer capability, project velocity, debt dynamics, agent capability and price, and bug costs, and compare them with a human-only baseline. Results: Escaped bugs are the dominant cost driver, and 61% of the agent budget goes to finding bugs. Agent capability matters more than token price, since higher-quality outputs reduce downstream quality assurance costs. In teams with capable agents, human developers mostly fix bugs and leave the implementation of new features to the agents. Teams with high-capability agents are typically cheaper than human-only teams, but low-capability agents offer no consistent advantage. At realistic velocities, the optimal teams still spend more on developers than on agents. Conclusions: There is neither a universal token budget per developer nor a universal agentic team structure. As in traditional development, this depends on many factors and teams need to be carefully tailored to the project context to achieve the optimal cost-quality trade-off.

  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI enhancement unavailable (incomplete_output). Original arXiv metadata is preserved.

Method: AI enhancement unavailable; see the original abstract.

Result: AI enhancement unavailable; see the original abstract.

Conclusion: AI enhancement unavailable (incomplete_output). Original arXiv metadata is preserved.

Objective: We determine how teams should divide spending between human developers and AI agents to deliver the features a project demands at the lowest total cost. Method: We model mixed teams of human developers and AI agents with eight specialized roles as a discrete-time stochastic process covering bug injection and detection, technical debt, human supervision of agents, and release cycles with feature freezes. Using Monte Carlo simulation and evolutionary search, we determine cost-optimal teams for 432 scenarios varying developer capability, project velocity, debt dynamics, agent capability and price, and bug costs, and compare them with a human-only baseline. Results: Escaped bugs are the dominant cost driver, and 61% of the agent budget goes to finding bugs. Agent capability matters more than token price, since higher-quality outputs reduce downstream quality assurance costs. In teams with capable agents, human developers mostly fix bugs and leave the implementation of new features to the agents. Teams with high-capability agents are typically cheaper than human-only teams, but low-capability agents offer no consistent advantage. At realistic velocities, the optimal teams still spend more on developers than on agents. Conclusions: There is neither a universal token budget per developer nor a universal agentic team structure.
